cards.back: They attach metadata to code in a form the compiler checks, instead of in comments or external files
cards.extra: Comments cannot be validated or processed. An annotation is a type, so a misspelled or misapplied one fails at compile time.
cards.example:
@interface Note { String value(); }
class Ex {
  @Note("compiler-checked metadata") int field;
}

cards.front: What does @Override actually protect you from?
cards.back: A signature mistake that would otherwise silently create a new method
cards.extra: Without it, tostring() compiles as an unrelated method and your override never runs. With it, the compiler says there is nothing to override.
cards.example:
class Base { void run() {} }
class Ex extends Base {
  @Override void run() {}
}

cards.front: What is @SuppressWarnings for, and what is the risk?
cards.back: Silencing a compiler warning at a specific scope — at the risk of hiding a real problem
cards.extra: It should be narrow and justified. Suppressing at class level turns off the warning everywhere, including where it was right.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
  java.util.List raw() { return new java.util.ArrayList(); }
}

cards.extra: @Target says where it may be applied; @Retention says whether it survives to the class file or runtime. Without retention RUNTIME, reflection cannot see it.

cards.back: Class-level annotations marked @Inherited are visible to subclasses; method and field annotations are never inherited
cards.extra: The book calls this out explicitly. Frameworks that look like they inherit do so by walking the hierarchy themselves.
cards.example:
class Ex extends Base { boolean inherited = getClass().isAnnotationPresent(Mark.class); }
@interface Mark {} // without @Inherited
@Mark class Base {}

cards.front: What can an annotation element's type be?
cards.back: Primitives, String, Class, enums, annotations, or arrays of those — never a general object
cards.extra: Elements are compile-time constants, which is why default values must be literals. This restriction is what lets annotations live in the class file.
cards.example:
enum E { A }
@interface Inner {}
@interface M { int i(); String s(); Class c(); E e(); Inner inner(); int[] nums(); }
@M(i=1, s="x", c=String.class, e=E.A, inner=@Inner, nums={1,2}) class Ex {}
